text:
Chapter four. The currency trap.

There's a layer most European investors completely forget. The dollar.

More than seventy percent of your world ETF is priced in dollars. When the dollar falls against the euro, you lose money, even if American stocks don't move at all.

Here's a simple example. Say an American stock stays exactly flat in dollars for a year. But the euro rises ten percent. In euros, you just lost about nine percent. On a stock that didn't move.

And here's a very common misunderstanding. Many people buy the euro listed version of their ETF and think the currency risk is gone. It isn't.

What matters is not the currency you pay with. It's the currency the underlying companies are priced in. Apple is a dollar company, whether you buy it in Frankfurt, Milan, or New York.

And in the dot-com crash, that's exactly what happened.

In October 2000, one euro was worth just eighty-three cents. By the end of 2004, it was worth one dollar thirty-six.

For a euro investor, that move alone wiped out almost forty percent of the value of every dollar asset.

Look at 2002. World stocks lost about twenty percent in dollars. In euros, they lost thirty-three.

Then 2008 did the opposite. In the panic, investors ran to the dollar, and the dollar rose. That cushioned the crash: minus forty-one percent in dollars, but minus thirty-seven in euros.

And this isn't ancient history. In 2025, the dollar fell sharply against the euro. World stocks gained around twenty percent in dollars, but only about seven percent for a euro investor.

So in a crash, the currency can be your airbag, or your second punch. And you don't get to choose in advance.

Right now, the euro is around one dollar thirteen, its lowest level since May 2025, after both the Fed and the E C B raised rates in September.

If the dollar falls back from here while US stocks fall too, euro investors get hit twice.

Over the very long run, currency swings tend to wash out. Over five or ten years, they can decide whether you made money or not.

Euro hedged share classes remove this risk. But they cost a bit more, and they also remove the airbag. There's no free lunch here.
